book.statusEvidence: Class 9 in this project uses Ganita Manjari (NCF-SE 2023 series, codes iemh1/iemh2, two parts). Class 10 has only jemh1 — the pre-NCF rationalised Mathematics book, carrying the NCERT rationalisation note. The NCF-aligned Class 10 replacement is not published on ncert.nic.in as of this download.
book.uncertainty: Whether a NCF-aligned Class 10 book arrives before authoring completes is unknown. Evidence missing: an official NCERT announcement of the Class 10 replacement date. Third-party sites claim 2027-28 but are not primary sources and were not relied on.
book.watermark: Pages carry a diagonal "Not to be republished" watermark — reinforces that Pragati authors original instruction and reproduces no textbook text.

sections.mathematicalIntent: Frame the chapter against Class IX real numbers; announce divisibility of positive integers as the route. NOTE: the body still advertises 'Euclid's division algorithm' in §1.2, which rationalisation removed — residual text.

State the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic from building numbers as products of primes; establish uniqueness of prime factorisation and apply it to HCF/LCM problems. 2 theorems, 4 examples, Exercise 1.1.

Prove irrationality of root 2, root 3, root 5 and of root p for prime p, using FTA via the lemma 'p divides a squared implies p divides a'. Proof by contradiction is the reasoning demand. 6 theorem blocks, 3 examples.
Recapitulate FTA, the divisibility lemma and the irrationality proofs. Carries Exercise 1.2 and a NOTE TO THE READER. REVIEW role.

chapters.progressionEvidence: Class 9 proved root 2 irrational by contradiction; Class 10 generalises the method and adds the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic as the justifying tool.

sections.mathematicalIntent: Recall polynomial, degree, and the linear/quadratic/cubic naming from Class IX; distinguish polynomials from non-polynomial expressions such as 1/(x-1).

sections.exactTitle: Geometrical Meaning of the Zeroes of a Polynomial
sections.mathematicalIntent: Read zeroes of a polynomial off its graph: value p(k), the parabola shapes for a>0 and a<0, and the x-coordinates where the graph meets the x-axis. Graph interpretation is the representation demand; exact grid coordinates matter.

sections.exactTitle: Relationship between Zeroes and Coefficients of a Polynomial
sections.mathematicalIntent: Establish the relationship between zeroes and coefficients of a quadratic polynomial (sum = -b/a, product = c/a) by factorisation; verify on examples and construct a quadratic from given sum and product. 4 examples, Exercise 2.1.
Recapitulate degree naming, the graphical meaning of zeroes and the zero-coefficient relations. Carries Exercise 2.2. REVIEW role.

chapters.progressionEvidence: Class 9 treated linear polynomials and their graphs; Class 10 extends to zeroes of higher-degree polynomials read geometrically.

chapters.exactTitle: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

sections.mathematicalIntent: Motivate a pair of linear equations from a contextual situation (rides and Hoopla) where one equation leaves the answer undetermined.

sections.exactTitle: Graphical Method of Solution of a Pair of Linear Equations
sections.mathematicalIntent: Solve a pair graphically; define consistent, inconsistent and dependent pairs and relate the three outcomes to intersecting, parallel and coincident lines, with the coefficient-ratio conditions. 3 examples, Exercise 3.1.

sections.exactTitle: Algebraic Methods of Solving a Pair of Linear Equations
sections.mathematicalIntent: Solve a pair algebraically. Numbered subsections 3.3.1 Substitution Method and 3.3.2 Elimination Method; motivated by non-integral intersection coordinates where graphing is unreliable. 7 examples, Exercises 3.2 and 3.3.
Recapitulate graphical and algebraic methods and the consistency classification. REVIEW role.

chapters.progressionEvidence: Class 9 solved and graphed pairs of linear equations and classified the three outcomes; Class 10 adds substitution/elimination at Class 10 scale.

sections.mathematicalIntent: Motivate the quadratic equation from a contextual area problem, connecting back to the quadratic polynomial of Chapter 2.

Define the standard form ax squared + bx + c = 0 with a not zero; identify quadratic equations and form them from situations. Carries the historical note on Sridharacharya, Al-Khwarizmi and Brahmagupta. 2 examples, Exercise 4.1.

sections.exactTitle: Solution of a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
sections.mathematicalIntent: Solve a quadratic by splitting the middle term and factorising; interpret roots against the original situation (rejecting inadmissible values). 3 examples.

Determine the nature of roots from the discriminant b squared minus 4ac, and solve using the quadratic formula where real roots exist. 5 examples, Exercise 4.2. The quadratic formula is taught here although no section is named for it.
Recapitulate standard form, factorisation, the quadratic formula and the discriminant conditions. Carries Exercise 4.3. REVIEW role.

chapters.progressionEvidence: No quadratic-equation solving in the verified Class 9 record; the object is named and solved here for the first time.

sections.mathematicalIntent: Motivate arithmetic progressions from patterns in nature and in daily life (salary increments, savings).
Define AP by constant common difference d; identify a and d, test whether a list is an AP, and write terms from a and d. 2 examples, Exercise 5.1.
Derive the nth term a + (n-1)d and apply it to find a term, a position, or an unknown among a, d, n. 8 examples, Exercise 5.2.

sections.exactTitle: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
sections.mathematicalIntent: Derive the sum of the first n terms by pairing/reversal, as n/2 times (2a + (n-1)d) and n/2 times (a + l); apply to daily-life totals. 6 examples, Exercises 5.3 and 5.4.
Recapitulate AP, nth term and sum formulae. REVIEW role.

chapters.progressionEvidence: Class 9 Chapter 8 established AP, nth term a+(n-1)d and the pairing sum; Class 10 formalises and extends the same objects — NOT a first introduction.

sections.mathematicalIntent: Contrast congruence (Class IX) with similarity: same shape, not necessarily same size; motivate indirect measurement of heights and distances.

Define similar figures; establish that similarity of polygons requires BOTH equal corresponding angles AND proportional corresponding sides, with counterexamples where only one holds. 1 activity, Exercise 6.1.

Prove the Basic Proportionality Theorem (Theorem 6.1) and its converse (6.2), using the equal-area argument on triangles with the same height. 6 theorem blocks, 3 examples, 2 activities, Exercise 6.2.
Establish the AAA/AA, SSS and SAS similarity criteria and apply them to prove triangles similar and compute unknown lengths. 5 theorem blocks, 5 examples, 3 activities, Exercise 6.3.
Recapitulate similarity definitions, BPT and the similarity criteria. REVIEW role.

chapters.progressionEvidence: Class 9 treated congruence; similarity and the Basic Proportionality Theorem are new named content.

sections.mathematicalIntent: Recall abscissa, ordinate and the forms (x,0) and (0,y) from Class IX as the basis for measuring in the plane.
Derive the distance formula from the Pythagoras relation by completing a right triangle; apply to collinearity, to types of quadrilateral, and to equidistant-point problems. 5 examples, Exercise 7.1.

Derive the section formula for internal division in ratio m1:m2, and obtain the midpoint as its special case; apply to dividing a segment and to finding a ratio. 5 examples, Exercise 7.2. Area of a triangle is absent from this edition.
Recapitulate distance from origin, distance between two points and the internal section formula. REVIEW role.

chapters.progressionEvidence: Class 9 Chapter 1 derived the distance formula and the midpoint; Class 10 adds the section formula — distance is REVISION, not introduction.

sections.mathematicalIntent: Motivate right triangles from contextual situations (tower, balloon) where an unmeasurable length must be found.

Define sine, cosine, tangent, cosecant, secant and cotangent as ratios of sides with respect to an acute angle; establish that the ratios depend on the angle and not on the triangle's size, and derive relations among them. 1 theorem block, 5 examples.

sections.exactTitle: Trigonometric Ratios of Some Specific Angles
sections.mathematicalIntent: Derive the ratios for 30, 45 and 60 degrees from the equilateral and isosceles right triangles, and motivate the values at 0 and 90 degrees by a limiting argument. 3 examples, Exercises 8.1 and 8.2.
Prove the identity sin squared A + cos squared A = 1 and derive the secant and cosecant identities from it; apply to proving simple identities. 4 examples, Exercise 8.3.
Recapitulate ratio definitions, specific-angle values and the identities. REVIEW role.

chapters.progressionEvidence: Trigonometric ratios are not in the verified Class 9 record.

sections.mathematicalIntent: Apply trigonometric ratios to heights and distances: define line of sight, angle of elevation and angle of depression, and solve contextual problems. 7 examples, Exercise 9.1. Spans ten of the chapter's eleven pages — the chapter has no Introduction section.
Recapitulate line of sight, elevation and depression. REVIEW role.

chapters.progressionEvidence: Applies Chapter 8 to heights and distances; no new mathematical object.

sections.mathematicalIntent: Recall the circle and its chord, segment, sector and arc from Class IX; set up the question of a line's possible positions relative to a circle.

Define the tangent as the line meeting a circle at exactly one point, reached as the limiting position of a secant; prove that the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. 1 theorem block, 3 activities.

sections.exactTitle: Number of Tangents from a Point on a Circle
sections.mathematicalIntent: Establish that no tangent exists from an interior point, exactly one from a point on the circle and exactly two from an exterior point, and prove the lengths of the two tangents from an external point are equal. 5 theorem blocks, 3 examples, 1 activity, Exercises 10.1 and 10.2.
Recapitulate the tangent definition and the two proved theorems. REVIEW role.

chapters.progressionEvidence: Class 9 Chapter 5 proved chord and angle properties; tangents are new, on an established circle foundation.

sections.exactTitle: Areas of Sector and Segment of a Circle
sections.mathematicalIntent: Define sector and segment; derive arc length and sector area as the theta/360 share of circumference and disc area, and obtain segment area by subtracting the triangle. 2 examples, Exercise 11.1. The chapter has no Introduction section.
Recapitulate arc length, sector area and segment area formulae. REVIEW role.

chapters.progressionEvidence: Class 9 Chapter 6 derived sector area and arc length; Class 10 extends to segments and combinations.

sections.mathematicalIntent: Recall cuboid, cone, cylinder and sphere from Class IX and motivate solids formed by combining them.

sections.exactTitle: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
sections.mathematicalIntent: Compute the surface area of a combination of two solids by adding the exposed curved/flat surfaces, recognising which faces are lost at the join. 4 examples, Exercise 12.1. Figures carry the dimensions required for the computation.

sections.exactTitle: Volume of a Combination of Solids
sections.mathematicalIntent: Compute the volume of a combination of solids by adding component volumes, noting that volumes add where surfaces do not. 3 examples, Exercise 12.2.
Recapitulate the combination method for surfaces and volumes. REVIEW role. Frustum and conversion-of-solids are absent from this edition.

chapters.progressionEvidence: Class 9 Chapter 14 established cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere and hemisphere; Class 10 combines them — surfaces and volumes are NOT first met here.

sections.mathematicalIntent: Recall grouped and ungrouped frequency distributions and their graphs from Class IX; set up the problem of a measure of central tendency for grouped data.
Compute the mean of grouped data by the direct, assumed-mean and step-deviation methods, using class marks, and justify when each is convenient. 5 examples, 2 activities, Exercise 13.1.
Define the modal class and derive the mode of grouped data from the modal-class formula; contrast mean and mode as answers to different questions. 7 examples, 2 activities, Exercise 13.2.

Derive the median of grouped data from cumulative frequency and the median-class formula; compare mean, median and mode. 2 examples, Exercise 13.3. The ogive appears only as a passing mention, not as taught content in this edition.
Recapitulate the three measures and their grouped-data formulae. REVIEW role.

chapters.progressionEvidence: Class 9 Chapter 10 established mean and weighted mean; Class 10 extends to grouped data, mode and median.

sections.mathematicalIntent: Define theoretical (classical) probability as favourable outcomes over equally likely outcomes; treat impossible and sure events, complementary events, and the 0-to-1 range; apply to coins, dice, cards and marbles. 21 examples, Exercise 14.1 — the whole instructional chapter is this one section.
Recapitulate the classical definition, the range and complementary events. Carries the NOTE contrasting experimental and theoretical probability. REVIEW role.

chapters.progressionEvidence: Class 9 Chapter 7 established the theoretical approach, sample space and equally likely outcomes; Class 10 continues the same treatment.

cbseCurriculum.prescribedTextbook: Mathematics - Textbook for class X - NCERT Publication
cbseCurriculum.redesignStatement: redesigned in alignment with NEP 2020 and NCF-SE 2023
scopeConstraints: Real Numbers: FTA stated after review/illustration; proofs of irrationality of root2, root3, root5 required
Triangles: BPT is (Prove); its converse and the AAA, SSS, SAS similarity criteria are State (without proof)
Trigonometry: proof of existence (well-definedness) of ratios; values at 30, 45, 60; ratios at 0 and 90 motivated
Trigonometric identities: prove sin2A+cos2A=1; only simple identities
Heights and distances: at most two right triangles; angles only 30, 45, 60
Areas related to circles: segment problems restricted to central angles 60, 90, 120
Surface areas and volumes: combinations of any TWO of cube, cuboid, sphere, hemisphere, right circular cylinder/cone
Statistics: mean, median, mode of grouped data; bimodal situations avoided
Probability: classical definition; simple problems only
Quadratic equations: only real roots; factorisation and quadratic formula
Coordinate geometry: distance formula and section formula (internal division) only

reconciliation.textbookVsCbse: The textbook remains source truth; CBSE scope is recorded alongside, never by deleting sections.
findings: CBSE prescribes solving by the quadratic formula; the textbook teaches it inside 4.2/4.4 with no section named for it.
CBSE does NOT list decimal expansions of rationals or Euclid division; §1.1 still advertises "Euclid's division algorithm in Section 1.2", which rationalisation removed — residual framing text.
The ogive / cumulative frequency curve survives only as a passing mention in §13.1 and the §13.5 summary; it is not prescribed and is not taught as content.
Area of a triangle by coordinates is absent from the textbook, consistent with CBSE scope.
Frustum and conversion of solids are absent from the textbook, consistent with CBSE "combinations of any two".
§6.4 is PARTIALLY_CURRENT: the textbook proves similarity criteria that CBSE prescribes as State (without proof).

verifiedVisually.actual: sin 0, 1/2, 1/root2, root3/2, 1; cos 1, root3/2, 1/root2, 1/2, 0; tan 0, 1/root3, 1, root3, not defined; cosec, sec, cot as reciprocals
verifiedVisually.checked: every entry read from the rendered table and verified against the standard values

verifiedVisually.actual: root 2 = r/s then a/b coprime; b root2 = a; 2b squared = a squared; a = 2c; b squared = 2c squared. Example 5 repeats it for root 3 with 3b squared = a squared
verifiedVisually.checked: proof structure read visually; contradiction step intact
